answer.label: Not Napoleon Bonaparte — a Victorian wordplayer's palindrome
answer.authorName: An anonymous American wordsmith (“J.T.R.” of Baltimore)
answer.authorDates: fl. 1848 · identified only by initials in a New York periodical
answer.sourceLine: Napoleon died in 1821 and never wrote English wordplay; this palindrome first surfaces in July 1848, credited to a “J.T.R.” of Baltimore, and was only pinned on Napoleon about a decade later as a fabricated anecdote riffing on his exile to Elba ↗.

source.excerpt: Able was I ere I saw Elba.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ locates the first appearance in the July 1848 Gazette of the Union, which credits an anonymous “J.T.R.” of Baltimore — not Napoleon.
QI finds the emperor ascription only by March 1858, in a Richmond newspaper anecdote it judges “spurious ↗,” fabricated for amusement.
Wikipedia likewise records that in 1848 “a certain ‘J.T.R.’ coined” the line, which “became famous after it was (implausibly) attributed to Napoleon ↗.”
source.excerptNote: The line is a palindrome: reversed letter-for-letter it reads the same. Its charm comes from tying the wordplay to Napoleon’s 1814 exile to the island of Elba — but that link is the invention of a later anecdotist, not Napoleon.

sourceLink.text: Quote Investigator: the 1848 origin and 1858 reassignment

source.rightsNote: The wording is first documented in an 1848 U.S. periodical — well before 1931 — so the palindrome itself is in the public domain in the United States. It was published anonymously (“J.T.R.”) and carries no surviving rights holder.

author.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
author.heading: About the misattributed name
author.metaLine: 1769–1821 · Emperor of the French, exiled to Elba in 1814
author.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was the French general and emperor whose 1814 abdication sent him into exile on the Mediterranean island of Elba — the historical hook that makes this palindrome so tempting to pin on him. But Napoleon was a native Italian-Corsican and French speaker who died in 1821, decades before the English line was ever recorded, and there is no evidence he composed English wordplay of any kind.

misattribution.heading: How Napoleon got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most durable false attributions in the English language — and the timeline makes the error plain.

items.why: Popular retellings say Napoleon uttered the line in exile — sometimes to his physician Dr. O’Meara. But Napoleon died in 1821, and the palindrome is not documented until July 1848 ↗. English was not his language, making English wordplay implausible.
The 1848 Gazette of the Union credits the line to a contributor who, “during some moments of leisure, had produced the following line” — identified only as “J.T.R.” ↗, not the emperor.

misattribution.truthLine: The palindrome cleverly uses Napoleon’s Elba exile as its theme — but it was written by an anonymous American wordsmith in 1848 and only reassigned to Napoleon around 1858 ↗ as an amusing invention.

context.heading: Why the fake stuck
lead: A good misattribution needs a good story, and this one is nearly perfect: a fallen emperor, marooned on Elba, ruefully punning on his own downfall in a sentence that reads the same backwards and forwards. It is too neat to resist — which is exactly why it spread.

The reality is more prosaic. The line is a feat of 19th-century recreational wordplay, printed in an American family periodical in 1848 and credited to an anonymous hobbyist. Only later did an anecdotist graft it onto Napoleon, and the improved version buried the original.
detailsBody: A palindrome reads identically in both directions. “Able was I ere I saw Elba” is prized as one of the finest in English because it is a grammatical, meaningful sentence — not just a string of letters — and its meaning cleverly evokes the very exile it is (falsely) said to describe.
context.pull: The palindrome uses Napoleon’s exile — it was not written by him.
